notes.meaning: The family record begins with Issachar, listing four of his direct sons: Tola, Puah, Jashub, and Shimron. These four men became the founding heads of the main clans in this northern tribe. Their names match the earlier list given when Moses counted the people before they entered the promised land.

Tola had six sons who served as chiefs over their family lines. By King David's time, these families had grown into an army of 22,600 brave warriors. God blessed this hardworking tribe so that they could defend their nation when called upon.

Uzzi's line produced Izrahiah and four sons, who were counted together as five leading chiefs. Because these families had many wives and children, their household troops numbered 36,000 ready soldiers. Their large households gave them the strength to field a powerful force in times of war.

Across all the clans of Issachar, the total number of valiant fighting men reached 87,000 in their official registers. This large sum shows how rapidly the tribe expanded over the centuries. A quiet and industrious life on the land helped them grow strong and numerous.

The writer turns to the tribe of Benjamin, listing three chief sons: Bela, Becher, and Jediael. Earlier records name more sons, but these three became the primary branches preserved in the later registers. Benjamin was known for producing fierce and skilled fighters.

Bela's branch included five family leaders who were celebrated for their courage in battle. In their official family book, they counted 22,034 soldiers fit for service. Even though Benjamin was a small territory, its clans maintained strong military readiness.

Becher had nine sons whose names became heads of important houses within Benjamin. Some of their names, such as Anathoth and Alemeth, were later given to Benjamite towns. Their registered descendants totaled 20,200 capable warriors.

Jediael's line continued through Bilhan, whose seven sons became recognized leaders of their households. These families produced 17,200 trained troops ready for conflict. Together, these Benjamite lists show a tribe that had recovered its strength after suffering heavy losses in earlier generations.

A brief note mentions the Shuppites and Huppites through Ir, alongside the Hushites from Aher. These names connect back to branches of Benjamin and perhaps provide a subtle pointer to the neighboring tribe of Dan. The ancient records preserved these smaller clans even when full details were missing.

The record briefly lists four sons of Naphtali, who were grandsons of Rachel's servant Bilhah. Unlike the other tribes, no counts of their later descendants or warriors are given here. Many of their detailed family registers were likely lost during the exile.

These verses record the western half-tribe of Manasseh living west of the Jordan River. Manasseh's family included Asriel and Machir, the father of Gilead, born through an Aramean concubine. Machir married into the neighboring clans, and the line also produced Zelophehad, who was famous for having only daughters who received an inheritance.

Machir's wife Maacah gave birth to Peresh and Sheresh, whose descendants included Ulam and Bedan. Bedan is remembered as a notable leader in Gilead and may be the same deliverer mentioned elsewhere in Israel's history. These families helped settle and protect the frontier lands of Joseph's descendants.

Gilead's sister Hammolecheth bore three notable sons, including Abiezer, whose family later produced the judge Gideon. Shemida's line is also recorded with four sons. These notices show how closely linked the leaders of Manasseh were across several generations.

The genealogy of Ephraim traces several generations down to Ezer and Elead. A tragic event is recorded where men from the Philistine city of Gath killed these sons during a raid over livestock. Whether the Ephraimites were raiding or defending their own animals, the conflict brought sudden death to the household.

Ephraim wept and mourned for his fallen sons over many days, and his relatives came to comfort him in his sorrow. Later, his wife bore another son whom he named Beriah, a name that sounds like the word for tragedy, because of the disaster that had struck his home. God graciously granted new life, yet the family never forgot the pain of their loss.

Ephraim's female descendant Sheerah achieved great honor by building and fortifying Upper and Lower Beth-horon, along with Uzzen-sheerah. These towns sat along key travel routes and military passes in Israel. Her work showed how a capable woman could bring lasting strength and protection to her tribe.

Another branch of Ephraim's family is traced through several generations to Elishama, who led the tribe during the wilderness wanderings. The line then continues through Nun to Joshua, who led Israel into the promised land. Despite the early tragedy in Ephraim's house, God raised up from this very tribe the commander who brought the nation into its rest.

The writer outlines the settlements of Ephraim, stretching from Bethel and Naaran in the east to Gezer in the west, and reaching up to Shechem. Each major town included surrounding farming villages that depended on it. This fruitful hill country formed the heartland of Ephraim's inheritance.

Along the northern border of Manasseh stood major fortress cities like Beth-shean, Taanach, Megiddo, and Dor on the coast. Together with Ephraim's towns, these settlements belonged to the broader house of Joseph. God gave this double tribe fertile and strategic land across the center of Canaan.

The record turns to the northern coastal tribe of Asher, naming four sons and their sister Serah. Naming a daughter was rare in ancient genealogies, showing that Serah held a special place of honor among the people. These founders established the initial clans of Asher.

Beriah's branch produced Heber and Malchiel, who founded the town of Birzaith. Heber's family included three sons and another named daughter, Shua. These notices preserve the names of leaders who developed communities in Asher's fertile coastal hills.

Heber's sons Japhlet and Shemer passed down their lineage through multiple sons of their own. Each son led an extended household that formed a division within the tribe. These records kept alive the memory of each family's heritage after the return from Babylon.

Helem, the brother of Shemer, had four sons, and his son Zophah fathered eleven sons of his own. This large list demonstrates how God made Asher fruitful and strong over the generations. Their households provided stability and leadership for the northern frontier.

The list concludes Asher's family lines with the sons of Jether and Ulla. These men led smaller branches of the tribe that remained closely tied to the main clan. Even lesser-known family names were valued and carefully preserved in Israel's sacred history.

All these men of Asher were recognized as heads of their households, choice warriors, and top commanders. Their military register numbered 26,000 men ready for battle. Though smaller than some other tribes, their leaders were chosen for quality and steadfast courage.
